China set to lead world in energy investment in 2026, CCTV says
article:
(Nov 8): China is expected to invest US$940 billion in energy in 2026, the most by any country, according to the Global Energy Transition Report 2026 released by the China Enterprise Reform and Development Society, China Central Television reported Sunday.

China had 2.337 billion kilowatts of installed renewable power capacity at the end of 2025, accounting for 60.1% of its total power capacity and 63.6% of new renewable installations globally, according to CCTV. Renewable generation reached 3.99 trillion kilowatt-hours, or 38.3% of the country’s power output, while additional renewable generation fully covered the increase in electricity consumption.

China’s energy investment focus is increasingly shifting from rapid capacity expansion towards grids and other infrastructure needed to integrate its renewable buildout. The International Energy Agency expects the country’s grid investment to rise to about US$140 billion in 2026.

Coal-fired power’s share of Chinese electricity generation fell to 49.7% in the first half of 2026, dropping below 50% for the first time, the report said. China’s energy-related carbon dioxide emissions declined 0.5% in 2025, while the country supplied 70% of the world’s wind-power equipment and 80% of its photovoltaic equipment, according to CCTV.

title: China raises delegate count to 2,360 for 2027 party congress
article:
(Nov 8): China set a quota of 2,360 delegates for the Communist Party’s 21st national congress in 2027, 60 more than for the previous gathering, Xinhua News Agency reported Sunday, citing the party’s Organization Department.

The delegates will be chosen through 38 electoral units, unchanged from the previous congress. The party said allocations will be based mainly on the number of party organisations and members, while also taking previous congresses’ allocations into account, said Xinhua.

The congress, held every five years, sets China’s broad political direction and selects the party’s Central Committee, making it a key event in determining the country’s top leadership.

The latest rules say the proportion of female delegates from provinces should generally account for no less than their share of local party membership. All 31 provincial-level delegations to the previous congress ultimately exceeded that share, according to an official post-election account.

The rules also call for greater representation of workers in newer forms of employment, such as those working in the digital economy.

Delegates are chosen through 38 electoral units covering regions and parts of the party-state system. Candidates are nominated from grassroots party organisations and vetted through successive levels before party congresses or representative meetings hold the final elections, with contested ballots required to have more than 15% more candidates than seats.
